An inverse problem asks which inputs to a system (settings, compositions, model parameters) produce a desired set of outputs, the reverse of a forward problem in which outputs are predicted or measured from known inputs. A few models can be inverted analytically, but most are inverted numerically: one fits a forward model and searches over inputs with an optimizer, fits a backward model that maps outputs directly to inputs, or uses statistical approaches such as Bayesian inversion. Inverse problems can be ill-posed, with no solution for some outputs or several inputs giving the same output, so a method suited to one problem may fail on another.

## Exhaustive enumeration for crystal design (2016)

Calfa and Kitchin posed materials design as the inverse of a kernel regression model whose inputs are a crystal's space group and element counts, so any solution is directly a composition and structure ([Calfa 2016](/papers/calfa2016/)). Because these inputs are discrete the problem is combinatorial, and as a first approach they enumerated every valid combination of predictor values present in the data, predicting properties for each and then filtering for targets such as a band gap near 1.23 eV or bounded Fermi levels. For 746 binary metal oxides this produced 1,153,504 candidates in about 19.7 h, including compositions absent from the training data; the authors note that model error can hide known crystals and present the cost as motivation for optimization-based formulations like those of computer-aided molecular design. Summary: [calfa2016](/papers/calfa2016/).

## Inverse mapping by AD and the implicit function theorem (2023)

Alves, Kitchin and Lima computed inverse maps for process models without optimization ([Alves et al. 2023](/papers/alves2023/)). With a model written in JAX, automatic differentiation gives the Jacobian, the implicit function theorem converts it into derivatives of the inputs with respect to the outputs, and these are integrated with a fourth-order Runge-Kutta scheme along the discretized boundary of a target output region, starting from one known point, to trace the boundary of the input region that achieves it. For a CSTR design problem the traced boundary enclosed every brute-force grid point mapping into the target, and for a methane aromatization membrane reactor the result matched an IPOPT-based NLP inversion to within about 0.02% average relative difference while running in 0.93 min, compared with 17.84 min for a cold-start NLP with finite differences and 1.97 min for a warm-start NLP with AD derivatives. The input region found was non-convex even for a circular output target, and the authors flag singular Jacobians at bifurcations as a case needing arc-length continuation. This is the AD-based method later cited in the 2025 Comment below. Summary: [alves2023](/papers/alves2023/).

## Conventional and generative routes compared (2025)

Kitchin compared four ways to find the RGB LED settings on the Claude-Light instrument that give a target count in three light-sensor channels ([Kitchin 2025](/papers/kitchin2025a/)). A linear forward model inverted with a minimizer and a partial least squares backward model gave the same answer as two [generative models](/papers/topics/generative-models/) (a Gaussian mixture model and a ForestDiffusion flow-matching model) used by conditioning on the desired outputs and generating the inputs. He contrasts the trade-offs: the forward-plus-optimizer route needs an initial guess and can find multiple solutions from different guesses; the backward model is evaluated directly but must be built around the specific outputs to be fixed and fails for many-to-one mappings; and the generative models can condition on any subset of variables and give sample-based uncertainty. All of the data-driven methods returned confident but physically impossible or wrong inputs when asked for outputs outside the training data. The study covered only a linear, one-to-one case. Summary: [kitchin2025a](/papers/kitchin2025a/).

## Automatic differentiation for inverse problems (2025)

Kitchin, Alves and Laird list inverse problems among the uses of [differentiable programming](/papers/topics/differentiable-programming/) outside ML training, citing an AD-based approach that maps two state spaces onto each other and that they describe as more efficient than conventional nonlinear programming formulations ([Kitchin et al. 2025](/papers/kitchin2025/)). The Comment gives no further detail on the method. Summary: [kitchin2025](/papers/kitchin2025/).

## Spectra-to-structure and generative design (2018)

Kitchin's 2018 Comment on ML in catalysis points to two ML routes to inverse problems ([Kitchin 2018](/papers/kitchin2018/)). One inverts XANES measurements: thousands of candidate structures and their simulated spectra are generated, and a model is trained to map spectral features back to structure, an idea he notes could extend to any spectroscopy that can be simulated from a structural model. The other is generative design of molecules, in which a molecule is encoded in a continuous representation, optimized there and decoded back; he suggests it could help homogeneous catalysis and notes no analogue yet for solid-state materials, nanoparticles or process conditions. Summary: [kitchin2018](/papers/kitchin2018/); see also [Generative models](/papers/topics/generative-models/).
